title: API rate limiter
prompt: Design the rate limiter for a public REST API. The API runs on 40 stateless servers behind a load balancer and handles 100,000 requests a second at peak from about 1 million API keys. Free keys may make 100 requests a minute and paid keys 10,000, and some expensive endpoints have tighter limits of their own. A request over its limit gets HTTP 429 with a header saying when to retry. The limiter may add at most 5 ms to a request.
explanation: Forty servers share one budget per key, so the counters must live somewhere shared, and checking them must be atomic and nearly free. The design turns on the algorithm you pick and on what happens when the counter store is down.

requirements: Limits per API key by plan, plus per-endpoint limits, answering 429 with Retry-After or rate limit headers
States the latency budget and decides what happens when the limiter itself is down: fail open or fail closed
Says how exact the limits must be, accepting a little overshoot in exchange for speed
estimation: 100,000 checks a second at peak, so the counter store needs 100,000 to 200,000 operations a second
About 1 million keys with a few counters each at around 100 bytes is a few hundred megabytes, which fits in memory
One Redis node handles on the order of 100,000 simple operations a second, so a few shards give headroom
api_data_model: An internal check taking key, endpoint and cost, returning allowed, remaining and reset time
Counter keys such as rate:{apiKey}:{endpoint}:{window} with a TTL equal to the window
Plan and endpoint limits kept in a config store and cached on each API server
architecture: The limiter runs as middleware on each API server or at the gateway, before the request handler
Counters live in a shared store such as Redis, because the load balancer spreads one key across 40 servers
Names an algorithm (token bucket, sliding window log or sliding window counter) and why it fits
scalability: Makes the check atomic in one round trip, with a Lua script or INCR with EXPIRE
Shards counters by API key so all of one key's counters live on one node
Cuts round trips for very busy keys by giving servers small local token allowances, accepting slight overshoot
reliability: Fails open when the counter store is unreachable and explains why that suits a public API
Weighs fixed windows (simple, but double bursts at the boundary) against sliding windows or token buckets
Avoids clock skew between servers by using window keys or the counter store's clock
communication: Walks one request through the check to either the handler or a 429
Explains the fixed-window boundary burst with a concrete example
